title: Acid-base & electrolyte crises: ABG stepwise, delta ratio, K⁺/Na⁺ emergencies
subject: Medicine
anchor: Never read pH alone: primary disorder → expected compensation → anion gap (albumin-corrected) → delta ratio → urine AG / urine Cl⁻
HAGMA = ketones, lactate, toxic alcohols, uraemia, salicylate; NAGMA = diarrhoea vs RTA (urine anion gap)
Hyperkalaemia + ECG change → IV calcium first (stabilises membrane, does not lower K⁺)
Chronic hyponatraemia: correct slowly (pons dies); hypernatraemia: correct slowly (brain swells)
algorithm:
ABG: pH <7.35 acidaemia | >7.45 alkalaemia → identify primary change (HCO₃⁻ vs PaCO₂)
→ Metabolic acidosis: Winter's expected PaCO₂ = 1.5 × HCO₃⁻ + 8 ± 2
  actual > expected → coexisting respiratory acidosis
  actual < expected → coexisting respiratory alkalosis
→ AG = Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻); normal ≈ 12 (8–16); add 2.5 for each 1 g/dL albumin below 4
  High AG → delta ratio = (AG − 12) / (24 − HCO₃⁻)
    <0.4 pure NAGMA | 0.4–0.8 HAGMA + NAGMA | 0.8–2 pure HAGMA
    >2 HAGMA + metabolic alkalosis (or pre-existing chronic respiratory acidosis)
    High AG → also check osmolar gap (>10 → methanol / ethylene glycol)
  Normal AG → urine AG = (UNa + UK) − UCl
    negative → GI HCO₃⁻ loss (diarrhoea) | positive → distal (type 1) RTA
→ Metabolic alkalosis: urine Cl⁻ <20 → saline-responsive (vomiting, NG suction, remote diuretics)
  urine Cl⁻ >20 → saline-resistant (hyperaldosteronism, Cushing, Bartter/Gitelman, current diuretic)

head: Primary disorder
Expected compensation
rows: PaCO₂ = 1.5 × HCO₃⁻ + 8 ± 2 (Winter's); roughly PaCO₂ ≈ last 2 digits of pH

tables.title: Electrolyte emergencies: what to do first
head: Crisis
Immediate step
Then
Limit / danger
rows: Calcium gluconate 10% 10 mL IV over 2–5 min (repeat if ECG unchanged; up to 30 mL acceptable); CaCl₂ in arrest
Shift: regular insulin 10 U + 25 g glucose (50 mL D50); salbutamol neb 10–20 mg; NaHCO₃ only if acidotic. Remove: loop diuretic, potassium binders (SZC, patiromer), haemodialysis (definitive)
Calcium does not lower K⁺; monitor glucose after insulin
3% NaCl 100 mL IV over 10 min, repeat up to 2 more times if symptoms persist
Target rise 4–6 mEq/L in first hours (enough to stop seizures/herniation)
Aim 4–6; never exceed 8 mEq/L/24 h in high-risk (exam answer); 10–12 is the absolute ceiling in standard risk. Overcorrection → re-lower with D5W ± desmopressin
Fall ≤10–12 mEq/L/24 h (≈0.5 mEq/L/h); faster → cerebral oedema

points: **HAGMA** causes (GOLDMARK): glycols, oxoproline (chronic paracetamol), L-lactate, D-lactate, methanol, aspirin, renal failure, ketoacidosis
**NAGMA**: diarrhoea, RTA, ureteral diversion, acetazolamide, saline overload (hyperchloraemic), Addison's
**Osmolar gap** = measured − (2Na⁺ + glucose/18 + BUN/2.8); >10 with HAGMA → methanol / ethylene glycol
**Salicylate** poisoning: mixed respiratory alkalosis (early, central) + HAGMA
**Vomiting**: hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis with paradoxical aciduria; urine Cl⁻ <20 → saline-responsive
Compensation never overshoots normal pH; a 'normal' pH with abnormal HCO₃⁻ and PaCO₂ = mixed disorder
Hyperkalaemia ECG sequence: peaked T → PR prolongation, flat/absent P → wide QRS → sine wave → VF/asystole
Pseudohyponatraemia (normal osmolality): hyperlipidaemia, paraproteinaemia; hyperglycaemia causes true translocational hyponatraemia (add 1.6 per 100 mg/dL glucose above 100)
ODS (central pontine myelinolysis): dysarthria, dysphagia, quadriparesis, locked-in, appears 2–6 days after overcorrection; risk ↑ with alcoholism, malnutrition, hypokalaemia, liver disease, Na⁺ ≤105

traps.stem: Acute severe asthma, RR 32: pH 7.38, PaCO₂ 40 mmHg, PaO₂ 65 mmHg. Patient is 'stable'?
traps.fix: A tachypnoeic asthmatic should have low PaCO₂ (<35). 'Normal' PaCO₂ = tiring respiratory muscles, impending hypercapnic failure → ICU, consider ventilation.

traps.stem: Septic ICU patient, albumin 1.0 g/dL: Na⁺ 140, Cl⁻ 108, HCO₃⁻ 20. AG = 12. NAGMA?
traps.fix: Correct for albumin: +2.5 × (4 − 1) = +7.5 → corrected AG 19.5 → occult HAGMA (likely lactate). Always albumin-correct the AG in hypoalbuminaemia.

traps.stem: Chronic hyponatraemia Na⁺ 110 in an alcoholic. How fast to correct?
traps.trap: 'Up to 12 mEq/L/day is allowed' (old standard-risk ceiling).
traps.fix: Alcoholism/malnutrition/hypokalaemia = high ODS risk → aim 4–6, never exceed 8 mEq/L in 24 h. Hypernatraemia rule is the reverse direction: rapid lowering → cerebral oedema.

cards.front: How does the urine anion gap separate causes of NAGMA?
cards.back:
UAG = (UNa + UK) − UCl.
Negative UAG → kidney is excreting NH₄⁺ (with Cl⁻) normally → GI HCO₃⁻ loss (diarrhoea).
Positive UAG → impaired distal acidification / NH₄⁺ excretion → distal (type 1) RTA.

cards.front: Order the ECG changes of rising K⁺ and name the first drug once they appear.
cards.back:
Peaked narrow T → PR prolongation with flattening/loss of P → QRS widening → sine wave → VF/asystole.
First drug: IV calcium gluconate 10% 10 mL over 2–5 min (membrane stabilisation; K⁺ unchanged).

cards.text: Chronic hyponatraemia correction: aim {{c1::4–6}} mEq/L/24 h; never exceed {{c2::8}} mEq/L/24 h in high-risk patients; overcorrection causes {{c3::osmotic demyelination syndrome}}, treated by re-lowering with {{c4::D5W ± desmopressin}}.
Metabolic alkalosis with urine Cl⁻ <20 mEq/L is {{c1::saline-responsive (vomiting, NG suction, remote diuretic)}}; urine Cl⁻ >20 with hypertension suggests {{c2::mineralocorticoid excess}}.

images.caption: Hyperkalaemia (K⁺ 8.2): tall, narrow-based peaked T waves — the earliest ECG sign; give IV calcium before anything else.

verify: Harrison 21e; hyponatraemia limits per US expert panel 2013 / European 2014 (≤8 mEq/L/24 h high risk); hyperkalaemia steps per UK Renal Association 2020.

title: Electrolyte disorders: K⁺, Na⁺ (SIADH/CSW/DI), Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺ & RTA types
subject: Medicine
anchor: Hypotonic hyponatraemia + euvolaemia + urine osm >100 + urine Na >30 → SIADH (after excluding hypothyroidism and cortisol deficiency)
Same labs but volume depleted after SAH/neurosurgery → cerebral salt wasting (give saline, not restriction)
Hypokalaemia + hypertension → mineralocorticoid excess (Conn, Liddle); normotensive + alkalosis → Bartter/Gitelman or diuretics
Hypokalaemia refusing to correct → check Mg²⁺
algorithm:
Hyponatraemia → serum osmolality
  Normal → pseudohyponatraemia (lipids, paraprotein) | High → hyperglycaemia, mannitol
  Low (true hypotonic) → urine osmolality
    <100 → primary polydipsia, beer potomania, tea-and-toast
    >100 → assess volume
      Hypovolaemic: UNa <20 → GI/skin loss | UNa >20 → diuretic, CSW, mineralocorticoid deficiency
      Euvolaemic: SIADH, hypothyroidism, glucocorticoid deficiency
      Hypervolaemic: CHF, cirrhosis, nephrotic (UNa <20) | renal failure (UNa >20)
Polyuria (>3 L/day) with dilute urine → water deprivation test
  Urine concentrates (osm >800) → primary polydipsia
  Stays dilute → desmopressin: urine osm ↑ >50% → central DI | little/no rise → nephrogenic DI

head: Feature
SIADH
Cerebral salt wasting
Diabetes insipidus
rows: Fluid restriction; oral urea / tolvaptan; 3% saline if severe symptoms
Central: desmopressin; nephrogenic: thiazide, low-salt diet (+ amiloride for lithium)

tables.title: Renal tubular acidosis types
head: Type 1 (distal)
Type 2 (proximal)
Type 4 (hypoaldosteronism)
rows: Low aldosterone or resistance → ↓ NH₄⁺ genesis
<5.5 once serum HCO₃⁻ falls below threshold
Sjögren, SLE, RA, amphotericin B, lithium, toluene
Fanconi syndrome, myeloma, acetazolamide, tenofovir, ifosfamide, Wilson
Diabetic nephropathy (hyporeninaemic), ACEi/ARB, spironolactone, trimethoprim, heparin, NSAIDs

points: **Bartter** (loop-like, NKCC2): hypercalciuria, young/antenatal; **Gitelman** (thiazide-like, NCC): hypocalciuria + hypomagnesaemia, milder, older
**Liddle** (ENaC gain of function): hypertension + hypokalaemia with LOW renin and LOW aldosterone; treat amiloride/triamterene (not spironolactone)
Hypokalaemia ECG: flat T, U waves, ST depression; IV K⁺ usually ≤10 mEq/h peripherally (up to 20 mEq/h centrally with monitoring)
Pseudohyperkalaemia: haemolysed sample, thrombocytosis, extreme leukocytosis, fist clenching
**Hypomagnesaemia** (PPIs, diuretics, alcohol, cisplatin, aminoglycosides) → refractory hypokalaemia and hypocalcaemia (↓PTH secretion and action)
Corrected Ca²⁺ = measured + 0.8 × (4 − albumin g/dL); hypocalcaemia → Chvostek, Trousseau, prolonged QT; hypercalcaemia → short QT
Severe symptomatic hypocalcaemia: IV calcium gluconate 10% 10–20 mL slowly, then infusion
Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis: hypokalaemic paralysis in young Asian men; give K⁺ cautiously + non-selective β-blocker (rebound hyperkalaemia)
Lithium is the commonest cause of acquired nephrogenic DI; hypercalcaemia and hypokalaemia also cause it

traps.stem: Post-SAH patient, Na⁺ 126, urine Na 80, postural hypotension, rising haematocrit. Fluid restrict?
traps.trap: Concentrated urine + high urine Na⁺ looks like SIADH → fluid restriction.
traps.fix: Volume depletion = cerebral salt wasting → isotonic saline ± fludrocortisone. Fluid restriction after SAH worsens vasospasm and ischaemia.

traps.stem: Young normotensive woman with hypokalaemic alkalosis, low urinary calcium and low Mg²⁺.
traps.fix: Low urine calcium + hypomagnesaemia = Gitelman (thiazide-like NCC defect). Bartter (loop-like) gives hypercalciuria.

traps.stem: Hypokalaemia (2.6) not rising despite 3 days of IV KCl in an alcoholic.
traps.fix: Check and replace magnesium first — hypomagnesaemia drives ROMK K⁺ wasting; K⁺ will not correct until Mg²⁺ does.

cards.front: Water deprivation test: urine stays dilute; after desmopressin urine osmolality rises by 60%. Diagnosis?
cards.back: Central (cranial) DI — kidneys respond to exogenous ADH (>50% rise). Little/no rise = nephrogenic DI; concentration during deprivation alone = primary polydipsia.

cards.text: Type {{c1::4}} RTA is the only RTA with {{c2::hyperkalaemia}}; its commonest cause is {{c3::hyporeninaemic hypoaldosteronism of diabetic nephropathy}}.
Distal (type 1) RTA: urine pH always {{c1::>5.5}}, {{c2::positive}} urine anion gap, and {{c3::nephrocalcinosis / calcium phosphate stones}}.

cards.front: Hypertension + hypokalaemia + low renin + low aldosterone. Diagnosis and drug?
cards.back: Liddle syndrome (ENaC gain-of-function, AD). Treat with amiloride or triamterene; spironolactone ineffective (not aldosterone-driven). DDx with same pattern: apparent mineralocorticoid excess (liquorice), CAH 11β-hydroxylase/17α-hydroxylase.

cards.text: SIADH vs CSW: both have high urine Na⁺; the discriminator is {{c1::extracellular volume status}} — CSW is {{c2::hypovolaemic}} and treated with {{c3::isotonic saline}}.

verify: Harrison 21e (fluid & electrolytes chapters); European hyponatraemia guideline 2014.

title: AKI & CKD: KDIGO staging, prerenal vs ATN, CKD-MBD, dialysis indications
subject: Medicine
anchor: AKI = creatinine ↑ ≥0.3 mg/dL in 48 h, or ≥1.5× baseline within 7 days, or urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 h
Prerenal: FeNa <1%, UNa <20, bland/hyaline casts; ATN: FeNa >2%, UNa >40, muddy-brown granular casts
Dialysis is indicated by AEIOU complications, not by a creatinine number
algorithm:
Rising creatinine / oliguria → stage by KDIGO
→ Prerenal? volume, BP, drugs (NSAID, ACEi/ARB, diuretics) → fluid challenge
→ Postrenal? bladder scan / USG KUB → catheter / relieve obstruction
→ Intrinsic? urine microscopy
  muddy-brown casts → ATN | RBC casts → GN (complement, ANCA, anti-GBM → biopsy)
  WBC casts / eosinophiluria + rash → AIN (stop drug ± steroids)
  dipstick blood + no RBCs → myoglobin (rhabdo; CK >5× ULN) → aggressive fluids
→ Urgent dialysis if refractory: Acidosis, Electrolytes (K⁺), Intoxication, Overload, Uraemia (pericarditis, encephalopathy, bleeding)

tables.title: KDIGO AKI staging
head: Stage
Serum creatinine
Urine output
rows: ≥3.0 × baseline OR ≥4.0 mg/dL OR start of RRT
<0.3 mL/kg/h for ≥24 h OR anuria ≥12 h

tables.title: Prerenal azotaemia vs acute tubular necrosis
head: Index
Prerenal
ATN
rows: Muddy-brown granular, tubular epithelial cell casts

points: Low FeNa despite intrinsic injury: contrast nephropathy, rhabdomyolysis, early obstruction, acute GN, hepatorenal syndrome
**CKD** = structural/functional abnormality >3 months; stage by GFR (G1 ≥90, G2 60–89, G3a 45–59, G3b 30–44, G4 15–29, G5 <15) and albuminuria (A1 <30, A2 30–300, A3 >300 mg/g)
eGFR: **CKD-EPI 2021** race-free creatinine (± cystatin C) equation is current standard (replaced MDRD)

**CKD-MBD**: phosphate retention + ↓1α-hydroxylase → ↓calcitriol, ↓Ca²⁺, ↑FGF-23 (earliest) → secondary hyperparathyroidism → osteitis fibrosa cystica; rugger-jersey spine; adynamic bone disease with oversuppression
CKD-MBD treatment: phosphate binders (sevelamer, lanthanum, calcium salts), active vitamin D, cinacalcet (calcimimetic), parathyroidectomy for tertiary
Renal anaemia: EPO deficiency, normocytic; replete iron first; avoid ESA targets above Hb 11.5 g/dL (↑ stroke/thrombosis)
**Contrast nephropathy**: creatinine rises 24–72 h; risk highest with eGFR <30, diabetes, volume depletion; prevent with isotonic IV saline; NAC and bicarbonate show no benefit (PRESERVE)
Metformin: hold at time of contrast if eGFR <30 or AKI; resume after 48 h if renal function stable
Dialysable toxins: salicylates, lithium, methanol, ethylene glycol, theophylline, valproate, metformin (lactic acidosis); NOT digoxin, TCA, benzodiazepines (protein-bound / large Vd)

traps.stem: AKI patient on furosemide: FeNa 3%. Diagnose ATN?
traps.fix: Diuretics raise FeNa artefactually; use FeUrea (<35% = prerenal).

traps.stem: CKD patient creatinine 7 mg/dL, asymptomatic, K⁺ 4.8, no overload. Start emergency dialysis?
traps.fix: Emergency dialysis needs a refractory complication (AEIOU: acidosis, hyperkalaemia, intoxication, overload, uraemic pericarditis/encephalopathy/bleeding). Planned dialysis in CKD is symptom-guided, usually eGFR 5–10.

traps.stem: Diabetic with eGFR 35 needs contrast CT. Best prophylaxis?
traps.trap: Oral N-acetylcysteine or sodium bicarbonate infusion.
traps.fix: Isotonic saline volume expansion, lowest dose iso-/low-osmolar contrast, stop nephrotoxins; NAC/bicarbonate not superior to saline.

cards.text: KDIGO AKI stage 3: creatinine ≥{{c1::3}}× baseline, or ≥{{c2::4.0 mg/dL}}, or {{c3::initiation of renal replacement therapy}}, or urine output <0.3 mL/kg/h for ≥{{c4::24 h}}.

cards.front: Muddy-brown granular casts in urine — diagnosis and typical FeNa?
cards.back: Acute tubular necrosis (ischaemic or nephrotoxic); FeNa >2%, urine Na >40, urine osm <350.

cards.text: In CKD, the earliest hormonal change of CKD-MBD is a rise in {{c1::FGF-23}}, followed by ↓calcitriol and {{c2::secondary hyperparathyroidism}}; the spine X-ray sign is {{c3::rugger-jersey spine}}.

cards.front: Urine dipstick strongly positive for blood but microscopy shows no RBCs after a crush injury. What and how to treat?
cards.back: Myoglobinuria from rhabdomyolysis (CK >5× ULN). Aggressive isotonic fluids targeting high urine output; treat hyperkalaemia; dialysis if refractory.

cards.text: Dialysis indications mnemonic AEIOU: {{c1::refractory acidosis}}, {{c2::electrolytes (hyperkalaemia)}}, {{c3::intoxications (e.g. lithium, methanol, salicylate)}}, {{c4::fluid overload}}, {{c5::uraemic pericarditis/encephalopathy}}.

title: DKA vs HHS: fluids, insulin, potassium thresholds & euglycaemic DKA
subject: Medicine
anchor: Young T1DM, abdominal pain, vomiting, Kussmaul breathing, fruity breath, HAGMA → DKA
Elderly T2DM, days of polyuria, glucose >600, osmolality >320, obtunded, little ketosis → HHS
Rule: fluids first; check K⁺ before insulin — K⁺ <3.3 → hold insulin and replace K⁺
SGLT2 inhibitor + ketoacidosis with near-normal glucose → euglycaemic DKA
algorithm:
Suspected DKA/HHS → glucose, ketones (β-hydroxybutyrate), VBG/ABG, AG, K⁺, osmolality, find precipitant (infection, missed insulin, MI)
→ FLUIDS: 0.9% NaCl 15–20 mL/kg (≈1–1.5 L) in hour 1
  then 0.45% NaCl if corrected Na⁺ normal/high, 0.9% if low
  add dextrose when glucose <250 mg/dL (DKA) / <300 (HHS) and continue insulin
→ POTASSIUM (before insulin):
  K⁺ <3.3 → HOLD insulin; give 20–30 mEq/h K⁺ until ≥3.3
  K⁺ 3.3–5.2 → 20–30 mEq K⁺ in each litre
  K⁺ >5.2 → no K⁺; recheck every 2 h
→ INSULIN: regular IV 0.1 U/kg/h (± 0.1 U/kg bolus); aim glucose fall 50–75 mg/dL/h
→ BICARBONATE only if pH <6.9 (ADA 2009; 2024 consensus: pH <7.0)
→ Resolution (DKA): glucose <200 + 2 of: HCO₃⁻ ≥15, venous pH >7.3, AG ≤12
  → overlap SC basal insulin 1–2 h before stopping the infusion

tables.title: DKA vs HHS (ADA criteria)
head: Feature
DKA
HHS
rows: Stupor / coma common; focal signs, seizures
Start only after initial fluids (fluids alone lower glucose); UK JBDS 0.05 U/kg/h

points: Serum K⁺ is often normal/high at presentation despite large **total-body K⁺ deficit** (acidosis + insulin lack shift K⁺ out); insulin will drop it fast
Corrected Na⁺ = measured Na⁺ + 1.6 × (glucose − 100)/100
Do not stop insulin when glucose normalises — add dextrose and continue until ketosis/acidosis resolves (closed AG)
Urine nitroprusside test detects acetoacetate, not β-hydroxybutyrate (the dominant ketone) — may under-read early and paradoxically rise during treatment
Phosphate replacement only if <1.0 mg/dL, cardiac dysfunction, respiratory depression or haemolytic anaemia

**Paediatric DKA cerebral oedema**: 4–12 h into treatment; headache, bradycardia + hypertension, falling GCS, incontinence; risks — young age, new-onset, severe acidosis, low PaCO₂, high urea, bicarbonate use; treat mannitol 0.5–1 g/kg or 3% saline
Paediatric (ISPAD): rehydrate over 24–48 h, insulin 0.05–0.1 U/kg/h started ≥1 h after fluids, no insulin bolus
**Euglycaemic DKA**: SGLT2 inhibitors, pregnancy, starvation, alcohol; glucose <250; give dextrose early alongside insulin; stop SGLT2i 3 days before elective surgery
Amylase/lipase and WBC may be raised in DKA without pancreatitis/infection

traps.stem: DKA: glucose 480, pH 7.1, K⁺ 3.0. First drug after starting saline?
traps.fix: K⁺ <3.3 → hold insulin, give IV K⁺ (20–30 mEq/h) until ≥3.3; insulin first can cause fatal hypokalaemic arrhythmia/respiratory muscle weakness.

traps.stem: Patient on empagliflozin, post-op vomiting, glucose 180 mg/dL, pH 7.15, HCO₃⁻ 10, β-OHB 5.
traps.trap: Glucose <250 so not DKA → look for lactic acidosis/sepsis.
traps.fix: Euglycaemic DKA from SGLT2i — treat as DKA with insulin plus early dextrose; stop the SGLT2 inhibitor.

traps.stem: 8-year-old, 6 h into DKA treatment, becomes drowsy with HR 52 and BP 140/90.
traps.trap: Hypoglycaemia or worsening acidosis; give bicarbonate.
traps.fix: Cerebral oedema — give mannitol (or 3% saline) immediately, reduce fluid rate, then imaging; bicarbonate is itself a risk factor.

cards.text: DKA potassium rule: K⁺ <{{c1::3.3}} → hold insulin and replace; K⁺ 3.3–5.2 → add {{c2::20–30 mEq}} per litre; K⁺ >{{c3::5.2}} → no K⁺, recheck in 2 h.
DKA insulin: regular IV {{c1::0.1 U/kg/h}}; add dextrose when glucose falls below {{c2::250 mg/dL}}; give bicarbonate only if pH <{{c3::6.9}}.

cards.front: Most important difference between HHS and DKA management?
cards.back: HHS: larger fluid deficit (~9 L) — fluids alone lower glucose, so start insulin only after initial fluid resuscitation (lower rate, e.g. 0.05 U/kg/h in UK JBDS); avoid rapid osmolality fall. Ketosis/acidosis minimal.

cards.front: Why can serum K⁺ be high in untreated DKA though the patient is K⁺ depleted?
cards.back: Insulin deficiency and hyperosmolality shift K⁺ out of cells while osmotic diuresis loses K⁺ in urine → normal/high serum K⁺ with total-body deficit; insulin unmasks the deficit.

cards.text: Euglycaemic DKA (glucose <250 mg/dL) is classically triggered by {{c1::SGLT2 inhibitors}}; treatment needs insulin plus {{c2::early dextrose}}.

title: Endocrine emergencies: adrenal crisis, thyroid storm, myxoedema coma, apoplexy, hypercalcaemia
subject: Medicine
anchor: Shock unresponsive to fluids + hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia, eosinophilia → adrenal crisis: hydrocortisone now, test later
Fever, AF, delirium, diarrhoea, jaundice after surgery/infection/iodine in a hyperthyroid → thyroid storm (Burch-Wartofsky ≥45)
Elderly hypothyroid woman in winter: hypothermia, hypoventilation, hyponatraemia, coma → myxoedema coma
Thunderclap headache + ophthalmoplegia + field loss in known adenoma → pituitary apoplexy
algorithm:
Adrenal crisis → draw cortisol + ACTH (do not wait) → hydrocortisone 100 mg IV bolus → 200 mg/24 h (50 mg 6-hourly or infusion) + 0.9% saline with dextrose → treat precipitant → taper
Thyroid storm → (1) propranolol (2) PTU (or methimazole) (3) iodine (Lugol/SSKI) ≥1 h AFTER thionamide (4) hydrocortisone (5) cooling, paracetamol (no aspirin) ± cholestyramine
Myxoedema coma → hydrocortisone first/with → IV levothyroxine 200–400 µg load (± T3) → passive rewarming, ventilate, correct Na⁺/glucose
Pituitary apoplexy → stress-dose hydrocortisone → MRI → transsphenoidal decompression if acuity/field loss or falling GCS; else conservative
Hypercalcaemic crisis (Ca >14 mg/dL) → IV 0.9% saline → calcitonin (hours) + zoledronic acid 4 mg IV (2–4 days) → denosumab if renal failure, steroids if vitamin-D mediated, dialysis if refractory

tables.title: Endocrine crises at a glance
head: Crisis
Key clue
First drug
Classic mistake
rows: Hypotension refractory to fluids, ↓Na⁺ ↑K⁺ ↓glucose; steroid withdrawal, sepsis, Waterhouse-Friderichsen
Waiting for ACTH stimulation test (if test needed later, dexamethasone does not cross-react with cortisol assay)
Thyroxine without steroid cover; active external rewarming (vasodilatory collapse)
Sudden headache, CN III palsy, bitemporal loss; triggers anticoagulation, dopamine agonist, pregnancy, surgery
Missing it as SAH; forgetting ACTH deficiency
Polyuria, dehydration, confusion, short QT; malignancy (PTHrP) or primary HPT

points: **Burch-Wartofsky** components: temperature, CNS dysfunction, GI-hepatic dysfunction, heart rate, heart failure, AF, precipitating event
**PTU** preferred in storm (also blocks peripheral T4 → T3 conversion); methimazole otherwise preferred (PTU hepatotoxic) except 1st trimester pregnancy
Avoid **aspirin** in thyroid storm — displaces T4 from TBG; use paracetamol
Primary adrenal insufficiency: hyperpigmentation + hyperkalaemia (mineralocorticoid loss); secondary: no hyperpigmentation, K⁺ normal
Sick-day rules for steroid users: double oral dose with fever; IM/IV hydrocortisone if vomiting
**Sheehan syndrome**: postpartum haemorrhage → pituitary necrosis; failure of lactation is the earliest clue
Apoplexy: commonest cranial nerve involved is **CN III**; MRI is the imaging of choice
Hypercalcaemia of malignancy: PTH suppressed, PTHrP high (squamous cell carcinoma lung, renal, breast); myeloma/osteolytic and lymphoma (calcitriol) other mechanisms
Calcitonin acts within hours but tachyphylaxis in ~48 h; bisphosphonates take 2–4 days — so give both

traps.stem: Thyroid storm: what is given first — Lugol's iodine or PTU?
traps.trap: Iodine first because it blocks hormone release fastest.
traps.fix: Thionamide first; iodine at least 1 h later. Iodine before blockade provides substrate and can worsen thyrotoxicosis (Jod-Basedow).

traps.stem: Panhypopituitarism with hypothyroidism found after pituitary surgery. Start levothyroxine today?
traps.trap: Replace thyroxine first to treat symptomatic hypothyroidism.
traps.fix: Replace glucocorticoid first — thyroxine increases cortisol clearance and can precipitate adrenal crisis.

traps.stem: Ca²⁺ 15.2 mg/dL, dehydrated and confused. First step?
traps.fix: Aggressive isotonic saline first; loop diuretics only after volume repletion if overload. Then calcitonin + zoledronic acid.

cards.text: Thyroid storm sequence: {{c1::β-blocker (propranolol)}} → {{c2::PTU/methimazole}} → {{c3::iodine ≥1 h later}} → {{c4::hydrocortisone}}; avoid {{c5::aspirin}}.
Adrenal crisis: give {{c1::hydrocortisone 100 mg IV}} immediately; if diagnostic testing is needed later, use {{c2::dexamethasone}} because it does not interfere with the cortisol assay.

cards.front: Postpartum woman fails to lactate after massive PPH, later amenorrhoea and fatigue. Diagnosis?
cards.back: Sheehan syndrome (ischaemic necrosis of the enlarged pituitary). Replace cortisol first, then thyroxine and other hormones.

cards.text: Burch-Wartofsky score ≥{{c1::45}} = thyroid storm highly likely; {{c2::25–44}} = impending storm.

cards.front: Why both calcitonin and zoledronic acid in hypercalcaemic crisis?
cards.back: Calcitonin lowers Ca²⁺ within hours but loses effect in ~48 h (tachyphylaxis); zoledronic acid takes 2–4 days but lasts weeks.

verify: Harrison 21e; ATA 2016 hyperthyroidism guideline; Endocrine Society adrenal insufficiency 2016.

title: Thyroid function patterns, hyperparathyroidism, MEN syndromes & pheochromocytoma
subject: Medicine
anchor: Low TSH + high FT4: diffuse ↑RAIU = Graves; hot nodule = toxic adenoma; LOW uptake = thyroiditis / exogenous / iodine
High Ca + high/inappropriately normal PTH + low phosphate → primary HPT (adenoma); very low urine Ca/Cr clearance ratio → FHH
Episodic headache, sweating, palpitations + hypertension → plasma free metanephrines; α-block before β-block
MTC + pheo + mucosal neuromas + marfanoid → MEN 2B (RET M918T)
algorithm:
Thyrotoxicosis (↓TSH ↑FT4/FT3) → TRAb ± RAIU / Tc scan
  Diffuse ↑uptake + TRAb+ → Graves (ophthalmopathy, pretibial myxoedema)
  Single hot nodule, rest suppressed → toxic adenoma | patchy → toxic MNG
  Low uptake → thyroiditis (painful + high ESR = subacute de Quervain; painless/postpartum), exogenous (low thyroglobulin), iodine load, amiodarone
Hypercalcaemia → PTH
  PTH high / inappropriately normal → 24-h urine Ca (Ca/Cr clearance <0.01 → FHH, no surgery) → sestamibi + USG → parathyroidectomy if indicated
  PTH suppressed → PTHrP (malignancy), vitamin D metabolites (granuloma, lymphoma), myeloma screen
Suspected pheochromocytoma → plasma free or 24-h urine fractionated metanephrines
  → CT/MRI adrenal → functional imaging (MIBG; ⁶⁸Ga-DOTATATE PET for metastatic/hereditary) → α-blocker 10–14 days → β-blocker → adrenalectomy

points: **Subacute (de Quervain) thyroiditis**: post-viral, painful tender thyroid, ↑ESR, low RAIU → NSAIDs/steroids + β-blocker; antithyroid drugs useless
Factitious thyrotoxicosis: low RAIU + LOW serum thyroglobulin (thyroiditis has high thyroglobulin)

**Primary HPT**: parathyroid adenoma ~85%; surgery if symptomatic or asymptomatic with Ca >1 mg/dL above ULN, eGFR <60, osteoporosis/vertebral fracture, stones/nephrocalcinosis/hypercalciuria, age <50
Secondary HPT (CKD, vitamin D deficiency): low/normal Ca, high PTH; tertiary: autonomous PTH after long secondary → high Ca and very high PTH
**FHH**: inactivating CASR mutation, mild hypercalcaemia, normal/mildly ↑PTH, urine Ca/Cr clearance ratio <0.01; benign, no parathyroidectomy
**Pheochromocytoma**: plasma free metanephrines most sensitive; ~35–40% hereditary (VHL, RET, NF1, SDHx) — old 'rule of 10s' obsolete; MRI T2 'light-bulb' bright
Preop: α-blockade (phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin) 10–14 days + high-salt/fluid intake, then β-blocker for tachycardia; post-op watch hypotension and hypoglycaemia
Thyroid FNAC (Bethesda) cannot separate follicular adenoma from carcinoma — needs capsular/vascular invasion on histology
Amiodarone thyrotoxicosis: type 1 (iodine-induced, ↑vascularity on Doppler → thionamide) vs type 2 (destructive thyroiditis, ↓flow → steroids)

traps.stem: Painful thyroid after a viral illness, ↓TSH ↑FT4, ESR 80, RAIU 2%. Start carbimazole?
traps.fix: Low-uptake destructive thyroiditis: hormone leaks from damaged follicles, no synthesis to block. Treat β-blocker + NSAID/prednisolone.

traps.stem: Pheochromocytoma with BP 210/120 and HR 130 before surgery. Start propranolol?
traps.fix: α-blockade first (phenoxybenzamine/doxazosin); β-blocker alone leaves α-vasoconstriction unopposed → hypertensive crisis/pulmonary oedema.

traps.stem: Mild hypercalcaemia (10.8), PTH upper-normal, family history of 'failed parathyroid surgery', urine Ca/Cr clearance 0.005.
traps.fix: Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia (CASR) — benign, surgery does not cure; ratio <0.01 is the clue.

cards.text: Thyrotoxicosis with low radioiodine uptake: {{c1::thyroiditis (subacute/painless/postpartum)}}, {{c2::exogenous thyroxine (low thyroglobulin)}}, iodine load, {{c3::struma ovarii (uptake in pelvis)}}.

cards.front: MEN 2B vs MEN 2A — which feature is absent in 2B and which is unique to it?
cards.back: 2B lacks hyperparathyroidism; unique: mucosal neuromas, marfanoid habitus, intestinal ganglioneuromatosis; MTC is earlier/more aggressive (thyroidectomy in first year).

cards.text: Pheochromocytoma: screen with {{c1::plasma free metanephrines}}; pre-op give {{c2::α-blocker (phenoxybenzamine/doxazosin)}} for 10–14 days, then {{c3::β-blocker}}.
FHH is caused by an inactivating mutation of the {{c1::calcium-sensing receptor (CASR)}} and is identified by a urine Ca/Cr clearance ratio <{{c2::0.01}}.

cards.front: Sick euthyroid syndrome — typical labs?
cards.back: Low T3 with high reverse T3 (↓ deiodinase-1), normal or low TSH, T4 low in severe illness. No thyroxine replacement; treat the illness.

title: Diabetes criteria & drugs, Cushing, Conn, acromegaly, prolactinoma, DI
subject: Medicine
anchor: Diabetes: FPG ≥126, 2-h OGTT ≥200, HbA1c ≥6.5% (confirm), or random ≥200 with symptoms
Cushing: confirm hypercortisolism first (DST/UFC/salivary), THEN ACTH, THEN localise
Hypertension + hypokalaemia (or resistant HTN) → aldosterone : renin ratio
Prolactinoma → cabergoline first, even macroadenoma with visual loss
algorithm:
Suspected Cushing (exclude exogenous steroid) → screen: 1 mg overnight DST (cortisol >1.8 µg/dL = fail), 24-h urinary free cortisol, late-night salivary cortisol
→ 2 abnormal → plasma ACTH
  ACTH low (<5 pg/mL) → adrenal source → CT adrenal (adenoma/carcinoma)
  ACTH normal/high → ACTH-dependent → pituitary MRI + high-dose DST / CRH test
    MRI adenoma (>6–10 mm) + concordant → Cushing disease → transsphenoidal surgery
    Equivocal → bilateral inferior petrosal sinus sampling (central:peripheral ACTH ≥2 basal, ≥3 after CRH = pituitary)
    Peripheral → ectopic ACTH (small cell lung, bronchial carcinoid) → CT chest/abdomen, DOTATATE PET
Primary aldosteronism → ARR high with suppressed renin → confirm (saline infusion / oral salt load / captopril) → CT adrenal → adrenal vein sampling
  Unilateral adenoma → laparoscopic adrenalectomy | bilateral hyperplasia → spironolactone / eplerenone

Mechanism
Key adverse effect / exam point
rows: GI upset, B12 deficiency, lactic acidosis; avoid eGFR <30; no hypoglycaemia
Genital mycotic infection, UTI, euglycaemic DKA, volume depletion, Fournier gangrene; proven HF & CKD benefit

points: Prediabetes: FPG 100–125 (IFG), 2-h OGTT 140–199 (IGT), HbA1c 5.7–6.4%
HbA1c misleading with haemolysis, recent transfusion, haemoglobinopathy, pregnancy, iron deficiency (falsely high)
Commonest cause of Cushing syndrome = exogenous steroids; of endogenous = pituitary adenoma (Cushing disease); ectopic ACTH → hypokalaemic alkalosis, pigmentation, rapid onset

**Conn's**: bilateral adrenal hyperplasia now the commonest cause; hypokalaemia only in a minority; AVS needed before surgery (CT misses microadenomas/incidentalomas); glucocorticoid-remediable aldosteronism → dexamethasone

**Acromegaly**: screen IGF-1; confirm failure of GH suppression after 75 g OGTT; MRI; transsphenoidal surgery → somatostatin analogue (octreotide), pegvisomant (GH-receptor antagonist), cabergoline; death mainly cardiovascular; screen colon (polyps)

**Prolactinoma**: commonest functioning pituitary adenoma; cabergoline > bromocriptine; 'hook effect' in huge adenoma → falsely low prolactin (dilute sample); stalk effect of non-functioning macroadenoma gives only modest ↑prolactin
Drug hyperprolactinaemia: antipsychotics (risperidone), metoclopramide, domperidone, methyldopa, verapamil; also primary hypothyroidism (TRH)
**DI**: central → desmopressin; nephrogenic (lithium, hypercalcaemia, hypokalaemia) → thiazide, amiloride for lithium; hypertonic-saline-stimulated copeptin is the newer test
Diabetes complications screening: retinopathy & nephropathy (urine ACR) at diagnosis in T2DM, 5 years after diagnosis in T1DM, then yearly

traps.stem: Macroprolactinoma (prolactin 2,500 ng/mL) with bitemporal hemianopia. Urgent surgery?
traps.fix: Cabergoline is first-line even with visual field loss — tumour shrinks within days–weeks; surgery for resistance/intolerance or apoplexy.

traps.stem: Confirmed primary aldosteronism, CT: 1.5 cm left adrenal nodule in a 55-year-old. Left adrenalectomy?
traps.trap: CT shows the adenoma, so remove it.
traps.fix: Adrenal vein sampling first — nonfunctioning incidentalomas are common; CT may mislead on lateralisation (may skip AVS only in <35 yr with clear unilateral adenoma).

traps.stem: Low ACTH with confirmed hypercortisolism. Next investigation?
traps.fix: Suppressed ACTH = ACTH-independent (adrenal) Cushing → CT adrenal. Pituitary MRI only if ACTH is normal/high.

cards.text: Diabetes diagnosis: fasting plasma glucose ≥{{c1::126 mg/dL}}, 2-h 75 g OGTT ≥{{c2::200 mg/dL}}, HbA1c ≥{{c3::6.5%}}.

cards.front: Which diabetes drug class is contraindicated with a family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma?
cards.back: GLP-1 receptor agonists (liraglutide, semaglutide) — thyroid C-cell tumours in rodents; avoid in personal/family MTC or MEN 2.

cards.text: Cushing workup: 1 mg overnight dexamethasone test fails if morning cortisol >{{c1::1.8 µg/dL}}; low ACTH → {{c2::adrenal}} cause; equivocal ACTH-dependent cases need {{c3::bilateral inferior petrosal sinus sampling}}.

cards.front: Best screening and confirmatory tests for acromegaly?
cards.back: Screen: serum IGF-1. Confirm: failure of GH suppression after 75 g oral glucose (OGTT). Then pituitary MRI.

cards.text: Primary aldosteronism is screened with the {{c1::plasma aldosterone : renin ratio}} and lateralised by {{c2::adrenal vein sampling}}; bilateral hyperplasia is treated with {{c3::spironolactone/eplerenone}}.

images.caption: Acromegaly facies: frontal bossing, widened thick nose, prominent cheekbones, thick lips, coarse facial lines — screen with IGF-1.

verify: ADA Standards of Care 2025; Endocrine Society Cushing 2008/2021 update, primary aldosteronism 2016, acromegaly 2014 guidelines.

title: Tropical fevers: severe malaria, dengue, scrub typhus, leptospirosis, enteric, chikungunya
subject: Medicine
anchor: Fever + impaired consciousness / hypoglycaemia / acidosis / jaundice / AKI in falciparum → severe malaria → IV artesunate
Fever settling on day 3–7 with abdominal pain, vomiting, rising Hct, falling platelets → dengue critical phase (plasma leak)
Painless black eschar in axilla/groin + lymphadenopathy → scrub typhus → doxycycline
Flood/sewer exposure + conjunctival suffusion + calf tenderness + jaundice + AKI → leptospirosis (Weil)
algorithm:
Acute febrile illness (India) → smear/RDT malaria, NS1/IgM dengue, CBC, LFT, creatinine, blood culture
→ Malaria + any severity criterion → IV artesunate 2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12, 24 h then daily (3 mg/kg if <20 kg) → oral full ACT once tolerating (≥24 h parenteral)
→ Dengue: no warning signs → oral fluids, paracetamol, daily CBC
  Warning signs → isotonic crystalloid 5–7 mL/kg/h × 1–2 h, then taper by Hct
  Hypotensive shock → 20 mL/kg crystalloid bolus over 15–30 min, reassess; colloid if refractory; bleeding → blood
→ Eschar / AUFI with no other cause → empirical doxycycline 100 mg BD (azithromycin in pregnancy/children <8 if preferred)
→ Leptospirosis suspicion → mild: doxycycline | severe: IV penicillin G or ceftriaxone
→ Enteric fever → blood culture (week 1) → outpatient azithromycin | inpatient/complicated: IV ceftriaxone

points: **WHO severe malaria**: impaired consciousness/coma, prostration, multiple convulsions, acidosis, hypoglycaemia, severe anaemia, renal impairment, jaundice, pulmonary oedema, significant bleeding, shock, hyperparasitaemia >10%

India (NCVBDC): uncomplicated falciparum → ACT (artesunate + SP; artemether-lumefantrine in North-East) + single-dose primaquine 0.75 mg/kg (gametocytocidal); vivax → chloroquine 3 days + primaquine 0.25 mg/kg/day × 14 days (check G6PD)
Quinine → hyperinsulinaemic hypoglycaemia, cinchonism, QT prolongation; artesunate → post-artesunate delayed haemolysis (check Hb 1–3 weeks later)
**Dengue warning signs**: abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, clinical fluid accumulation, mucosal bleed, lethargy/restlessness, liver >2 cm, rising Hct with rapid platelet fall
Dengue: prophylactic platelet transfusion not indicated without bleeding; avoid aspirin/NSAIDs/IM injections; critical phase lasts 24–48 h around defervescence
Scrub typhus eschar sits in hidden moist areas (axilla, groin, inframammary, waistline) — examine the whole body

Enteric fever: BASU — Blood culture wk 1, Antibody (Widal) wk 2, Stool wk 3, Urine wk 3–4; fluoroquinolone resistance high in India; ileal perforation (antimesenteric border of terminal ileum) in week 3; chronic carriers harbour bacteria in gallbladder
Typhoid vaccines: Typbar-TCV conjugate from 6 months; Vi polysaccharide ≥2 yr; oral Ty21a ≥6 yr
Leptospirosis chemoprophylaxis for high-risk exposure: doxycycline 200 mg once weekly; Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction can follow penicillin

traps.stem: Dengue day 5: fever has gone, platelets 40,000, Hct rising, abdominal pain. Patient 'improving' — discharge?
traps.fix: Defervescence marks the critical (leak) phase; warning signs → admit, crystalloids 5–7 mL/kg/h titrated to Hct and urine output.

traps.stem: Falciparum malaria, GCS 9, in a district hospital where only quinine and artesunate are available.
traps.fix: IV artesunate is drug of choice for severe malaria in adults and children (lower mortality than quinine); quinine only if artesunate unavailable.

traps.stem: Fever 2nd week, Widal TO 1:80. Diagnose typhoid?
traps.fix: Single low Widal titre is unreliable in endemic India (prior exposure/vaccination); blood culture is diagnostic; a fourfold rising titre is needed.

cards.text: Severe malaria: IV artesunate {{c1::2.4 mg/kg}} at 0, 12 and 24 h then daily; children <20 kg need {{c2::3 mg/kg}}; complete with {{c3::a full oral ACT course}}.
Scrub typhus is caused by {{c1::Orientia tsutsugamushi}}, transmitted by {{c2::larval trombiculid mites (chiggers)}}; hallmark sign {{c3::painless black eschar}}; drug {{c4::doxycycline}}.

cards.front: Fever, conjunctival suffusion without discharge, severe calf tenderness, jaundice and oliguria after floods. Diagnosis and reference test?
cards.back: Leptospirosis — Weil disease (jaundice + AKI ± haemorrhage). Reference serology: microscopic agglutination test (MAT); treat IV penicillin G / ceftriaxone.

cards.text: Enteric fever: most useful test in week 1 = {{c1::blood culture}}; most sensitive culture overall = {{c2::bone marrow}}; the commonest serious week-3 complication = {{c3::ileal perforation}}.

cards.front: List the dengue warning signs.
cards.back: Abdominal pain/tenderness, persistent vomiting, clinical fluid accumulation (ascites/effusion), mucosal bleeding, lethargy/restlessness, liver enlargement >2 cm, rising haematocrit with rapid fall in platelets.

title: HIV: NACO testing, first-line ART (TLD), OIs by CD4, prophylaxis & IRIS
subject: Medicine
anchor: Adult diagnosis in India = Strategy III (three different-principle/antigen assays); infant <18 months = HIV DNA PCR
Treat all: start TLD (tenofovir + lamivudine + dolutegravir) regardless of CD4, ideally within 7 days
Delay ART 4–6 weeks in cryptococcal (and TB) meningitis because of fatal IRIS
CD4 <200 PCP; <100 toxoplasma, cryptococcus; <50 CMV retinitis, MAC
algorithm:
HIV test (Strategy III) positive → baseline CD4, viral load, TB screen (symptoms/CXR), CrAg if CD4 <100–200, HBsAg, creatinine
→ Active OI?
  Cryptococcal / TB meningitis → treat OI, defer ART 4–6 weeks
  Pulmonary/other TB → start ATT, ART within 2 weeks (dolutegravir 50 mg BD with rifampicin)
  Otherwise → start TLD same day–7 days
→ Prophylaxis: cotrimoxazole (CD4 thresholds below); TB preventive therapy (INH 6 months or 3HP) once active TB excluded
→ Viral load at 6 and 12 months, then yearly
  VL >1000 copies/mL → enhanced adherence 3 months → repeat VL >1000 = virological failure → switch regimen

Infection

TB is the commonest OI and killer in India
Subacute dyspnoea, dry cough, exertional desaturation, bilateral perihilar ground-glass, ↑LDH

points: NACO: Strategy I for blood safety (single test), Strategy III for diagnosis; 4th-generation Ag/Ab assays detect p24 earlier (window ~2–3 weeks)
Infants exposed to HIV: DNA PCR (dried blood spot) at 6 weeks; maternal IgG makes antibody tests unreliable until 18 months
**Dolutegravir**: preferred in pregnancy now (early neural-tube concern resolved); raises serum creatinine by blocking tubular secretion (not true GFR loss); weight gain, insomnia

Drug toxicities: **TDF** — Fanconi-type proximal tubulopathy, bone loss; **abacavir** — hypersensitivity (test HLA-B*57:01); **efavirenz** — neuropsychiatric, vivid dreams; **nevirapine** — hepatotoxicity, SJS; **zidovudine** — anaemia, myopathy
Cotrimoxazole prophylaxis: classic/US threshold CD4 <200 (PCP), <100 with toxo IgG+ | NACO/WHO resource-limited setting: CD4 <350 or WHO stage 3–4
MAC prophylaxis (CD4 <50) no longer needed if ART is started immediately (current US guidance)

**IRIS**: paradoxical worsening of a treated OI or unmasking of a subclinical one, usually within weeks–3 months of ART; risk ↑ with very low CD4, high VL; continue ART, add NSAIDs/prednisolone (TB-IRIS)
PML (JC virus): non-enhancing asymmetric white-matter lesions without mass effect; no specific therapy — ART
Ring-enhancing lesion with CD4 <100 and toxo IgG+ → empirical anti-toxo therapy 2 weeks; no response → biopsy (lymphoma)

traps.stem: HIV, CD4 40, cryptococcal meningitis diagnosed today. When to start ART?
traps.fix: Defer ART 4–6 weeks after starting antifungal therapy; early ART increased mortality from cryptococcal IRIS (COAT trial).

traps.stem: Six-week-old infant of HIV-positive mother: HIV ELISA positive.
traps.trap: Infant is infected; start ART on ELISA alone.
traps.fix: Antibody may be maternal (persists up to 18 months). Diagnose with HIV DNA PCR; confirm with a second sample.

traps.stem: PLHIV on rifampicin-based ATT starting TLD.
traps.fix: Rifampicin induces UGT1A1/CYP3A → dolutegravir 50 mg twice daily during and 2 weeks after rifampicin.

cards.text: NACO first-line ART for adults: {{c1::TLD — tenofovir + lamivudine + dolutegravir}}, started {{c2::irrespective of CD4 count}}.
OI thresholds: PCP CD4 <{{c1::200}}; toxoplasma & cryptococcus CD4 <{{c2::100}}; CMV retinitis & MAC CD4 <{{c3::50}}.

cards.front: PCP in HIV: when are adjunctive corticosteroids indicated?
cards.back: Moderate–severe PCP: PaO₂ <70 mmHg on room air or A–a gradient ≥35 mmHg — start prednisolone within 72 h with cotrimoxazole.

cards.front: Define IRIS and its management.
cards.back: Inflammatory worsening of a known (paradoxical) or hidden (unmasking) infection as immunity recovers after ART, typically within weeks–3 months. Continue ART, treat the pathogen, NSAIDs or steroids for moderate–severe (e.g. TB-IRIS).

cards.text: Abacavir hypersensitivity is predicted by {{c1::HLA-B*57:01}}; tenofovir disoproxil causes {{c2::proximal tubulopathy (Fanconi) and bone loss}}.

title: Poisoning: OP, paracetamol, snakebite, celphos, toxic alcohols, toxidromes & antidotes
subject: Medicine
anchor: Pinpoint pupils + bronchorrhoea + sweating + fasciculations + bradycardia → organophosphate (opioid is dry, no fasciculations)
Atropinise to a CLEAR CHEST, HR >80, SBP >80, dry axillae — not to pupil size
Snakebite + unclotted 20WBCT → haemotoxic (viper) → ASV; ptosis/ophthalmoplegia → neurotoxic (cobra/krait)
Rotten-fish/garlic odour, refractory shock, silver nitrate paper blackens → aluminium phosphide
algorithm:
Snakebite (Indian national protocol) → reassure, immobilise limb, no tourniquet/incision → hospital
→ 20-minute whole blood clotting test (2 mL in new clean dry glass tube, undisturbed 20 min)
  Unclotted → haemotoxic envenomation → ASV
  Neuroparalysis (ptosis, bulbar weakness, respiratory failure) → ASV + airway/ventilation
→ ASV (polyvalent, Big 4): 8–10 vials IV over 1 h (neurotoxic and haemotoxic alike)
  Haemotoxic: repeat 20WBCT every 6 h; repeat ASV until blood clots
  Neurotoxic: no improvement after 1–2 h → one repeat dose; beyond that ventilate (more ASV futile)
  Neostigmine trial (with atropine) — helps post-synaptic cobra toxin, not krait
  Anaphylaxis to ASV → stop, adrenaline 0.5 mg IM, then restart slowly; no test dose
Organophosphate → decontaminate, airway → atropine 1.8–3 mg IV, double dose every 5 min to endpoints → infusion
  ± pralidoxime early (before 'ageing'), benzodiazepine for seizures

head: Poison
Antidote
rows: Fomepizole (or ethanol) + haemodialysis; folinic acid (methanol), thiamine + pyridoxine (EG)

points: **OP vs carbamate**: OP binds irreversibly and 'ages' (oximes useless after ageing); carbamate reversible, shorter, less CNS (poor BBB entry)
Pralidoxime (WHO regimen 30 mg/kg bolus then 8 mg/kg/h) reactivates AChE before ageing; benefit in trials is uncertain
**Intermediate syndrome** 24–96 h after OP: proximal limb, neck-flexor, cranial and respiratory weakness (atropine-resistant → ventilate); **OPIDN** after 2–3 weeks: distal motor neuropathy

**Paracetamol**: toxic dose >150 mg/kg; plot level ≥4 h post-ingestion on Rumack-Matthew nomogram; US treatment line 150 µg/mL at 4 h (UK 100-line); nomogram invalid for staggered/unknown-time ingestion
IV NAC 21-h regimen: 150 mg/kg over 1 h → 50 mg/kg over 4 h → 100 mg/kg over 16 h (300 mg/kg); near-complete protection if started within 8 h
King's College (paracetamol) transplant criteria: arterial pH <7.3 after resuscitation, OR INR >6.5 + creatinine >3.4 mg/dL + grade III–IV encephalopathy

Big 4 Indian snakes: cobra, common krait (neurotoxic; krait bites at night, painless, minimal local signs, abdominal pain), Russell's viper, saw-scaled viper (haemotoxic); Russell's viper → AKI, DIC, pituitary haemorrhage

**Aluminium phosphide (celphos)**: phosphine → mitochondrial poison, refractory shock, myocarditis, metabolic acidosis; no specific antidote — supportive, vasopressors, magnesium sulphate used; silver nitrate test turns black
**Methanol**: formic acid → 'snowfield' vision, optic disc hyperaemia, putaminal necrosis; **ethylene glycol**: calcium oxalate crystals, AKI, hypocalcaemia; both HAGMA + high osmolar gap

traps.stem: OP poisoning on atropine: pupils still pinpoint, HR 118, chest has crackles.
traps.trap: Tachycardia → stop atropine; or keep going until pupils dilate.
traps.fix: Endpoint is a clear chest (no bronchorrhoea), HR >80, SBP >80, dry axillae; tachycardia is not a contraindication when crackles persist. Pupil size is not a target.

traps.stem: Krait bite with ptosis and respiratory weakness — neostigmine trial will reverse it?
traps.fix: Krait β-bungarotoxin is presynaptic — neostigmine rarely helps; cobra (postsynaptic α-neurotoxin) responds. Krait needs ASV + ventilation.

traps.stem: Paracetamol overdose 2 h ago; level 120 µg/mL. Below line — discharge?
traps.fix: Levels before 4 h cannot be interpreted; repeat at 4 h. If >8 h or time unknown/staggered → start NAC immediately.

cards.text: Atropinisation endpoints in OP poisoning: {{c1::clear chest on auscultation}}, heart rate >{{c2::80/min}}, systolic BP >{{c3::80 mmHg}}, dry axillae, pupils no longer pinpoint.
Rumack-Matthew nomogram treatment line (US): {{c1::150 µg/mL}} at {{c2::4 h}}; IV NAC regimen lasts {{c3::21 h}} (150 → 50 → 100 mg/kg).

cards.front: How is the 20-minute whole blood clotting test done and interpreted?
cards.back: 2 mL venous blood in a new, clean, dry glass tube, left undisturbed 20 min, then tipped once. Unclotted = venom-induced consumption coagulopathy (viper) → ASV; repeat 6-hourly.

cards.text: Initial ASV dose in India: {{c1::8–10 vials}} IV over 1 h for both {{c2::neurotoxic and haemotoxic}} envenomation; anaphylaxis is treated with {{c3::adrenaline 0.5 mg IM}}.

cards.front: Antidote of methanol and why dialysis?
cards.back: Fomepizole (alcohol dehydrogenase inhibitor) or ethanol to block formic acid formation; haemodialysis removes methanol and formate (severe acidosis, visual signs, high levels); add folinic acid.

cards.front: Anticholinergic vs sympathomimetic toxidrome — single best discriminator?
cards.back: Skin: anticholinergic is hot and DRY ('dry as a bone'); sympathomimetic is hot and SWEATY. Both have mydriasis and tachycardia.

images.caption: Russell's viper: chain of dark-edged oval blotches along the back, triangular head — haemotoxic (VICC, AKI) → unclotted 20WBCT → ASV.

verify: Standard Treatment Guidelines: Management of Snakebite (MoHFW India 2017, national snakebite protocol); AIIMS/WHO OP guidance (Eddleston); UK/US paracetamol nomogram lines differ (100 vs 150).

title: Vasculitis (Chapel Hill), autoantibodies & antiphospholipid syndrome
subject: Medicine
anchor: Sinusitis/saddle nose + lung cavities + RPGN + c-ANCA (PR3) → GPA; same minus granuloma/ENT with p-ANCA (MPO) → MPA
Asthma + eosinophilia + mononeuritis multiplex → EGPA
HBV + mononeuritis + renal microaneurysms, lungs spared, ANCA-negative → PAN
>50 yr, new headache, jaw claudication, raised ESR → GCA: steroids before biopsy
algorithm:
Suspected vasculitis → define vessel size by clinical picture
  Large (aorta/branches): pulse deficit, BP difference, claudication → Takayasu (<40, Asian women) / GCA (>50)
    GCA + visual symptoms → IV methylprednisolone now; else prednisolone 40–60 mg → temporal artery biopsy/ultrasound (halo) within 1–2 weeks
  Medium: microaneurysms, infarcts, mononeuritis → PAN (angiography; HBsAg) | child with fever ≥5 days → Kawasaki → IVIG 2 g/kg + aspirin, echo
  Small: palpable purpura, GN, alveolar haemorrhage → ANCA, anti-GBM, complement, cryoglobulins, IgA
    ANCA + organ-threatening → glucocorticoid + rituximab or cyclophosphamide (± plasma exchange for severe renal/pulmonary haemorrhage) → maintenance rituximab/azathioprine

points: **ANA patterns**: homogeneous (anti-dsDNA, anti-histone), peripheral/rim (anti-dsDNA), speckled (Sm, RNP, Ro, La, Scl-70), nucleolar (systemic sclerosis), centromere (limited SSc)

**APS (revised Sapporo/Sydney 2006)**: ≥1 clinical (arterial/venous/small-vessel thrombosis; ≥1 fetal death ≥10 wk; ≥1 preterm birth <34 wk from pre-eclampsia/placental insufficiency; ≥3 consecutive miscarriages <10 wk) + ≥1 lab (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin IgG/IgM medium–high titre, anti-β2-glycoprotein I) positive twice ≥12 weeks apart
2023 ACR/EULAR APS classification uses weighted clinical and lab domains (research classification)
APS clues: thrombosis with paradoxically prolonged aPTT, thrombocytopenia, livedo reticularis, false-positive VDRL
APS treatment: warfarin INR 2–3 for thrombotic APS; avoid DOACs (especially triple-positive/arterial); pregnancy → LMWH + low-dose aspirin
Kawasaki is the commonest cause of acquired heart disease in children in developed countries; IVIG within 10 days of fever onset cuts aneurysm risk
HSP intussusception is typically ileo-ileal (idiopathic childhood is ileocolic)
Anti-GBM + ANCA double-positive patients behave like anti-GBM acutely and relapse like AAV

traps.stem: 70-year-old with new temporal headache, jaw claudication, ESR 95; biopsy available next week.
traps.trap: Wait for biopsy confirmation before steroids.
traps.fix: Start high-dose steroids immediately (IV methylprednisolone if visual loss); biopsy remains diagnostic for ~2 weeks after starting steroids.

traps.stem: HBV-positive man with mononeuritis multiplex, hypertension, abdominal pain; urine shows no RBC casts. MPA?
traps.fix: PAN: medium vessels, renal infarcts/microaneurysms (not glomerulonephritis), lungs spared, ANCA-negative, HBV-associated.

traps.stem: Triple-positive APS with arterial stroke. Switch warfarin to rivaroxaban for convenience?
traps.trap: DOACs are standard for VTE now.
traps.fix: DOACs had excess arterial events in triple-positive APS (TRAPS trial) → warfarin remains treatment of choice.

cards.text: {{c1::PR3}}-ANCA (c-ANCA) = GPA; {{c2::MPO}}-ANCA (p-ANCA) = MPA and EGPA; PAN is {{c3::ANCA-negative}} and linked to {{c4::hepatitis B}}.
Most specific antibody for SLE = {{c1::anti-Smith}}; the one that tracks nephritis/activity = {{c2::anti-dsDNA}}; drug-induced lupus = {{c3::anti-histone}}.

cards.front: Kawasaki disease: diagnostic criteria and treatment?
cards.back: Fever ≥5 days + ≥4 of 5: bilateral non-exudative conjunctivitis, oral changes (strawberry tongue, cracked lips), polymorphous rash, extremity changes (oedema → periungual desquamation), cervical lymph node ≥1.5 cm. Treat IVIG 2 g/kg + aspirin; echo for coronary aneurysm.

cards.text: APS lab criteria must be positive on two occasions at least {{c1::12 weeks}} apart: {{c2::lupus anticoagulant}}, anticardiolipin, {{c3::anti-β2-glycoprotein I}}.

cards.front: Anti-centromere vs anti-Scl-70?
cards.back: Anti-centromere → limited cutaneous SSc (CREST), late pulmonary arterial hypertension. Anti-Scl-70 (topoisomerase I) → diffuse SSc, interstitial lung disease.

points: **RA 2010 ACR/EULAR**: ≥6/10 from joints (0–5), serology RF/anti-CCP (0–3), acute-phase reactants (0–1), duration ≥6 weeks (0–1); methotrexate (+ folic acid) is the anchor DMARD

RA extras: atlanto-axial subluxation (flexion-extension films before intubation), Felty (RA + splenomegaly + neutropenia), Caplan (pneumoconiosis + nodules), ILD; leading cause of death is cardiovascular

**SLE EULAR/ACR 2019**: entry ANA ≥1:80 on HEp-2, then ≥10 weighted points with ≥1 clinical criterion; class III/IV nephritis (10) and anti-dsDNA/anti-Sm (6) weigh most; hydroxychloroquine for every patient (annual retinal screening after 5 yr)

**Drug-induced lupus**: procainamide (highest risk), hydralazine, isoniazid, minocycline, quinidine, anti-TNF; slow acetylators; anti-histone +, dsDNA usually − (except anti-TNF), complement normal, kidney/CNS spared; resolves on withdrawal

**Spondyloarthritis** (HLA-B27): inflammatory back pain <40 yr, sacroiliitis (MRI bone-marrow oedema earliest), bamboo spine, syndesmophytes, ↓Schober; anterior uveitis commonest extra-articular; NSAIDs first-line, then TNF/IL-17 inhibitors (MTX ineffective for axial disease)
Reactive arthritis: urethritis (Chlamydia) or dysentery → arthritis + conjunctivitis/uveitis, keratoderma blennorrhagicum, circinate balanitis; psoriatic: DIP, dactylitis, pencil-in-cup, nail pitting
**Sjögren**: dry eyes/mouth, parotid swelling, anti-Ro/La; Schirmer ≤5 mm in 5 min; lip biopsy focal lymphocytic sialadenitis (focus score ≥1); risk of MALT lymphoma; distal RTA
**Scleroderma renal crisis**: abrupt HTN + AKI + MAHA; treat ACE inhibitor (captopril) even if creatinine rises; high-dose steroids (>15 mg prednisolone) precipitate it
Do not stop allopurinol during an acute gout attack; starting it during an attack is acceptable with anti-inflammatory cover (ACR 2020)

traps.stem: Man on isoniazid with arthralgia, serositis, ANA+, anti-histone+, anti-dsDNA negative, normal complement. SLE?
traps.fix: Drug-induced lupus — anti-histone positive, dsDNA negative, normal complement, no renal/CNS disease; stop the drug.

traps.stem: Synovial fluid: rhomboid crystals, weakly positive birefringence, in an elderly knee.
traps.fix: CPPD (pseudogout); screen for hyperparathyroidism, haemochromatosis, hypomagnesaemia, hypothyroidism. Gout = needle-shaped strongly negative.

traps.stem: Diffuse SSc, new BP 190/110, creatinine rising after starting captopril. Stop the ACE inhibitor?
traps.fix: Continue/uptitrate ACE inhibitor — it is the life-saving therapy for scleroderma renal crisis; dialysis if needed.

cards.text: Monosodium urate crystals are {{c1::needle-shaped}} and {{c2::strongly negatively}} birefringent; CPPD crystals are {{c3::rhomboid}} and {{c4::weakly positively}} birefringent.

cards.front: SLE EULAR/ACR 2019 entry criterion and threshold?
cards.back: Entry: ANA ≥1:80 on HEp-2 cells (ever). Then classify as SLE with ≥10 weighted points including ≥1 clinical criterion (only the highest-weighted item per domain counts).

cards.text: Most specific test for RA = {{c1::anti-CCP antibody}}; anchor DMARD = {{c2::methotrexate}}; joint characteristically spared = {{c3::DIP}}.

cards.front: Ankylosing spondylitis: first-line drug and what fails for axial disease?
cards.back: NSAIDs first-line (+ exercise/physiotherapy). Conventional DMARDs (methotrexate, sulfasalazine) do not help axial disease → TNF or IL-17 inhibitors.

cards.text: Drug causing the highest risk of drug-induced lupus = {{c1::procainamide}}; marker antibody = {{c2::anti-histone}}; organs typically spared = {{c3::kidney and CNS}}.

title: Cirrhosis & portal hypertension: variceal bleed, SAAG, SBP, HRS, HE, scores, HCC
subject: Medicine
anchor: Cirrhotic with haematemesis → vasoactive drug + ceftriaxone + EVL within 12 h; NSBB only after the acute bleed
Ascites: SAAG ≥1.1 = portal hypertension; ascitic PMN ≥250/mm³ = SBP
Cirrhosis + ascites + AKI not improving after albumin and diuretic withdrawal, no shock/nephrotoxin/structural disease → HRS-AKI
Arterial hyperenhancement + washout in a cirrhotic nodule ≥10 mm = LI-RADS 5 = HCC without biopsy
algorithm:
Acute variceal bleed → 2 large-bore IV lines, restrictive transfusion (Hb trigger 7, target 7–9 g/dL), avoid over-filling
→ Start vasoactive drug at once: terlipressin 2 mg IV 4-hourly (or octreotide 50 µg bolus + 50 µg/h), continue 2–5 days
→ Antibiotic prophylaxis: IV ceftriaxone 1 g/day (up to 7 days)
→ IV erythromycin 250 mg 30–120 min pre-endoscopy (if no QT prolongation)
→ Endoscopy within 12 h: oesophageal varices → band ligation (EVL); gastric (GOV2/IGV1) → cyanoacrylate glue
→ High risk (Child C 10–13, or Child B >7 with active bleeding at endoscopy) → pre-emptive TIPS within 72 h (ideally <24 h)
→ Uncontrolled → balloon tamponade (Sengstaken-Blakemore/Minnesota) or oesophageal stent as bridge → rescue TIPS
→ After bleed controlled (vasoactive stopped) → secondary prophylaxis: NSBB (propranolol/carvedilol) + repeated EVL until eradication
points: **SAAG** = serum albumin − ascitic albumin: ≥1.1 g/dL → portal HTN (cirrhosis, cardiac, Budd-Chiari); with ascitic protein ≥2.5 → cardiac ascites / Budd-Chiari; SAAG <1.1 → peritoneal TB, carcinomatosis, pancreatic, nephrotic

**SBP**: ascitic PMN ≥250/mm³; usually monomicrobial E. coli/Klebsiella; treat cefotaxime/ceftriaxone + IV albumin 1.5 g/kg day 1 and 1 g/kg day 3; long-term norfloxacin/ciprofloxacin after first episode. Polymicrobial, protein >1 g/dL, glucose <50, high LDH → secondary peritonitis (surgical)
Large-volume paracentesis >5 L → albumin 6–8 g per litre removed (prevents post-paracentesis circulatory dysfunction)

**HRS-AKI** (ICA): no response after 2 days of diuretic withdrawal + albumin 1 g/kg, no shock, no nephrotoxins, no parenchymal disease → terlipressin + albumin (noradrenaline in ICU); cure = liver transplant

**Hepatic encephalopathy**: precipitants — GI bleed, infection, constipation, hypokalaemia/alkalosis, sedatives, dehydration, TIPS; lactulose to 2–3 soft stools/day; add rifaximin to prevent recurrence; ammonia level not needed for diagnosis; do not restrict protein
**MELD** (bilirubin, INR, creatinine; MELD-Na adds sodium; MELD 3.0 adds sex & albumin) ranks transplant priority; refer when MELD ≥15
**Alcoholic hepatitis**: Maddrey DF = 4.6 × (PT − control) + bilirubin; ≥32 (or MELD >20) → prednisolone 40 mg/day × 28 days if no infection/GI bleed; Lille score at day 7 >0.45 → stop steroids

**HCC**: surveillance USG ± AFP every 6 months in cirrhosis/high-risk HBV; LI-RADS LR-1 benign → LR-5 definite HCC, LR-M malignant non-HCC, LR-TIV tumour in vein; Milan criteria for transplant: single ≤5 cm or ≤3 nodules each ≤3 cm, no vascular invasion/extrahepatic spread
BCLC: very early/early → resection, ablation, transplant; intermediate → TACE; advanced → atezolizumab + bevacizumab; terminal → best supportive care

**Wilson disease** (ATP7B, chr 13): low ceruloplasmin, ↑24-h urine copper, Kayser-Fleischer rings (Descemet's membrane), acute liver failure with Coombs-negative haemolysis and low ALP; treat penicillamine/trientine, zinc

traps.stem: Cirrhotic vomiting blood, BP 90/60. Start propranolol to reduce portal pressure?
traps.trap: NSBB lowers portal pressure, so give it now.
traps.fix: Never in the active bleed — worsens hypotension and blunts compensatory tachycardia. Give terlipressin/octreotide + ceftriaxone + EVL within 12 h; NSBB only for secondary prophylaxis after control.

traps.stem: Ascitic fluid total WBC 400/mm³, 40% neutrophils, cirrhotic with fever.
traps.fix: The cutoff is the absolute PMN count: 400 × 0.4 = 160 <250 → not SBP. PMN ≥250 needed.

traps.stem: Cirrhotic with ascites, creatinine up from 1.0 to 2.4; on diuretics. Start terlipressin now for HRS?
traps.trap: Any AKI in cirrhosis with ascites = HRS.
traps.fix: First stop diuretics/nephrotoxins and give albumin 1 g/kg for 2 days, exclude shock and structural disease; only non-responders meet HRS-AKI criteria.

cards.text: Acute variceal bleed bundle: {{c1::terlipressin or octreotide}} + {{c2::IV ceftriaxone}} + {{c3::endoscopic band ligation within 12 h}}; NSBB {{c4::only after the bleed is controlled}}.
SAAG ≥{{c1::1.1 g/dL}} indicates portal hypertension; SBP is diagnosed by ascitic {{c2::PMN ≥250/mm³}} and treated with cefotaxime plus {{c3::IV albumin}}.

cards.front: Maddrey discriminant function: formula and action threshold?
cards.back: DF = 4.6 × (patient PT − control PT, seconds) + serum bilirubin (mg/dL). DF ≥32 = severe alcoholic hepatitis → prednisolone 40 mg/day × 28 days (if no contraindication); Lille >0.45 at day 7 → non-responder, stop.

cards.text: Milan criteria for transplant in HCC: single tumour ≤{{c1::5 cm}} or up to {{c2::3}} tumours each ≤{{c3::3 cm}}, with no vascular invasion or extrahepatic spread.

cards.front: Hepatitis B: which marker is the only one positive in the window period?
cards.back: IgM anti-HBc (HBsAg has cleared, anti-HBs not yet detectable).

images.caption: Wilson disease: golden-brown Kayser-Fleischer ring at the corneal limbus (copper in Descemet's membrane); slit-lamp confirms.
Cirrhosis: large spider naevi (central arteriole with radiating vessels, blanch on pressure) on the upper body — hyperoestrogenism of chronic liver disease.

verify: Baveno VII (2022); AASLD 2021 ascites/SBP/HRS guidance & ICA HRS-AKI 2015/2019; EASL 2018 decompensated cirrhosis; ACR LI-RADS v2018; BCLC 2022.

title: IBD (UC vs Crohn), IBS (Rome IV), coeliac, H. pylori & upper GI bleed scores
subject: Medicine
anchor: Bloody diarrhoea, continuous disease from rectum, mucosal only, p-ANCA, non-smoker → UC
Skip lesions, terminal ileum, transmural, fistulae, granulomas, smoker, ASCA → Crohn
Iron-deficiency anaemia refractory to oral iron + diarrhoea/bloating → anti-tTG IgA (with total IgA)
Upper GI bleed: Glasgow-Blatchford before endoscopy (score 0–1 = outpatient), Rockall after (mortality)
algorithm:
Acute severe UC (Truelove-Witts: ≥6 bloody stools/day + ≥1 of HR >90, T >37.8 °C, Hb <10.5 g/dL, ESR >30)
→ Admit; stool C. difficile + CMV, plain AXR (toxic megacolon: transverse colon >6 cm), VTE prophylaxis
→ IV hydrocortisone 100 mg 6-hourly (or methylprednisolone 60 mg/day)
→ Day 3: >8 stools/day, or 3–8 with CRP >45 (Travis/Oxford) → high colectomy risk
→ Rescue: infliximab or ciclosporin → no response by days 5–7 / megacolon / perforation → subtotal colectomy
Upper GI bleed → resuscitate (Hb trigger 7; 8 if cardiovascular disease) → Glasgow-Blatchford
  GBS 0–1 → outpatient endoscopy | higher → endoscopy within 24 h
  Forrest Ia/Ib/IIa (± IIb after clot removal) → endoscopic dual therapy → high-dose PPI 72 h
  Rebleed → repeat endoscopy → angio-embolisation / surgery

head: Feature
Ulcerative colitis
Crohn's disease
rows: Rectum, continuous proximal spread; colon only (backwash ileitis)
Mouth to anus; terminal ileum commonest; skip lesions
Crypt abscesses, crypt distortion, no granulomas
Friable mucosa, loss of vascular pattern, pseudopolyps
String sign of Kantor, fistulae, creeping fat
Toxic megacolon, PSC, higher colorectal cancer risk
Fistulae, strictures, perianal abscess, gallstones, oxalate stones, B12 deficiency

points: **Montreal**: Crohn — Age A1 ≤16, A2 17–40, A3 >40; Location L1 ileal, L2 colonic, L3 ileocolonic, L4 upper GI modifier; Behaviour B1 inflammatory, B2 stricturing, B3 penetrating, 'p' perianal. UC — E1 proctitis, E2 left-sided (distal to splenic flexure), E3 extensive
IBD treatment ladder: 5-ASA (UC), steroids for flares (not maintenance), azathioprine/MTX, biologics (anti-TNF, vedolizumab, ustekinumab), JAK inhibitors (UC)

**Rome IV IBS**: recurrent abdominal pain ≥1 day/week in last 3 months with ≥2 of — related to defecation, change in stool frequency, change in form; onset ≥6 months before; subtype by Bristol stool form; alarm features (age >50, weight loss, bleeding, anaemia, nocturnal symptoms, family history CRC/IBD) → investigate

**Coeliac**: anti-tTG IgA + total IgA (IgA deficiency → IgG DGP/tTG) on a gluten-containing diet; duodenal biopsy (≥4 from D2 + bulb): villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, intraepithelial lymphocytes (Marsh); HLA-DQ2/DQ8 has high negative predictive value; dermatitis herpetiformis; EATL risk; ESPGHAN no-biopsy route in children if tTG-IgA ≥10× ULN + EMA positive on second sample

**H. pylori tests**: urea breath test and stool antigen detect active infection and confirm cure; serology cannot (stays positive); invasive — rapid urease (CLO), histology, culture (sensitivity); stop PPI 2 weeks and antibiotics/bismuth 4 weeks before testing; test of cure ≥4 weeks after therapy
H. pylori associations: duodenal & gastric ulcer, intestinal-type gastric adenocarcinoma, gastric MALT lymphoma (low-grade may regress with eradication), ITP, unexplained iron deficiency
First-line eradication where clarithromycin resistance is high: bismuth quadruple (PPI + bismuth + tetracycline + metronidazole) for 14 days

**Glasgow-Blatchford**: urea, Hb, SBP, pulse, melaena, syncope, hepatic disease, cardiac failure — needs no endoscopy; **Rockall** full score needs endoscopic diagnosis and stigmata; AIMS65 predicts mortality
**Forrest**: Ia spurting, Ib oozing, IIa visible vessel, IIb adherent clot, IIc flat pigmented spot, III clean base — endotherapy for Ia, Ib, IIa

traps.stem: Suspected coeliac disease; patient already gluten-free for 3 months; tTG negative.
traps.fix: Serology and histology normalise on a gluten-free diet; re-challenge with gluten (≈6 weeks) before testing, or use HLA-DQ2/DQ8 to exclude. Also check total IgA.

traps.stem: H. pylori test of cure: serology negative? / urea breath test done while on omeprazole.
traps.trap: Serology confirms cure; PPI doesn't matter.
traps.fix: Use urea breath test or stool antigen ≥4 weeks after therapy, off PPI for 2 weeks — PPIs cause false negatives; serology stays positive for months.

traps.stem: Smoker with ulcerative colitis asks if stopping smoking will help.
traps.fix: Smoking is protective in UC (flares can follow cessation) but harmful in Crohn's — still advise cessation for general health; for Crohn's it is a disease-modifying intervention.

cards.text: Truelove-Witts acute severe UC: ≥{{c1::6}} bloody stools/day plus ≥1 of HR >{{c2::90}}, temperature >37.8 °C, Hb <{{c3::10.5 g/dL}}, ESR >30 mm/h; first-line treatment is {{c4::IV hydrocortisone}}.

cards.front: Crohn vs UC on barium: 'string sign' and 'lead-pipe' colon?
cards.back: String sign of Kantor = narrowed terminal ileum in Crohn's (spasm/stricture). Lead-pipe colon = loss of haustra in chronic UC.

cards.text: Coeliac screening test = {{c1::anti-tTG IgA}} together with {{c2::total serum IgA}}; gold standard = {{c3::duodenal biopsy (villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, IELs)}}.

cards.front: Which upper GI bleed score can be done before endoscopy and identifies patients safe for outpatient care?
cards.back: Glasgow-Blatchford score (urea, Hb, SBP, pulse, melaena, syncope, liver disease, heart failure); score 0 (≤1 in ESGE) → outpatient management.

cards.text: Rome IV IBS: abdominal pain at least {{c1::1 day per week}} for the last {{c2::3 months}} with ≥2 of: related to {{c3::defecation}}, change in frequency, change in form.

images.caption: Plain abdominal X-ray in ulcerative colitis: grossly dilated colon (transverse >6 cm) with loss of haustra = toxic megacolon → surgical emergency.

verify: BSG IBD 2019 & ECCO 2022; Rome IV (2016); ESPGHAN 2020 coeliac; Maastricht VI/Florence 2022 (H. pylori); ESGE 2021 non-variceal UGIB.

title: Glomerulopathies: nephritic vs nephrotic — LM, IF, EM & complement
subject: Medicine
anchor: Read every biopsy as a triad: light microscopy + immunofluorescence + electron microscopy, then add serum complement
Deposit site rule: subepithelial = membranous (spikes) & PSGN (humps); subendothelial = MPGN / lupus IV (wire loops); mesangial = IgA, HSP; intramembranous = dense deposit disease
Low C3 + low C4 = classical pathway (lupus, immune-complex MPGN/HCV-cryo, endocarditis); low C3 + normal C4 = alternative pathway (PSGN, C3 glomerulopathy)
Haematuria during a sore throat with normal C3 = IgA nephropathy; 1–3 weeks after with low C3 = PSGN
algorithm:
Glomerular disease suspected → urine: protein quantity + sediment
  Nephrotic (proteinuria >3.5 g/day, albumin <3 g/dL, oedema, lipiduria) → child: MCD → steroid trial without biopsy | adult: biopsy (anti-PLA2R if membranous suspected)
  Nephritic (RBC casts, haematuria, HTN, oliguria) → C3/C4, ASO/anti-DNase B, ANA/dsDNA, ANCA, anti-GBM, HBV/HCV, cryoglobulins
    Rapid rise in creatinine (days–weeks) → RPGN → urgent biopsy (crescents) → classify by IF:
      Linear IgG → type 1 anti-GBM → plasma exchange + steroids + cyclophosphamide
      Granular → type 2 immune complex (PSGN, lupus, IgA/HSP, MPGN)
      Pauci-immune → type 3 ANCA (GPA, MPA, EGPA) → steroids + rituximab/cyclophosphamide
    Low C3 persisting >8–12 weeks → not PSGN → think MPGN / C3 glomerulopathy / lupus

points: **Nephritic**: haematuria with RBC casts, HTN, oliguria, mild (<3.5 g) proteinuria — PSGN, IgA, RPGN, lupus. **Nephrotic**: >3.5 g/day proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, oedema, hyperlipidaemia, hypercoagulability (loss of antithrombin III)
Renal vein thrombosis: most frequent with membranous nephropathy
Crescents = proliferating **parietal epithelial cells** + monocytes/macrophages, triggered by fibrin leaking into Bowman's space; RPGN when crescents in >50% of glomeruli
PSGN serology: ASO after pharyngitis, anti-DNase B better after impetigo; low C3 beyond 8–12 weeks → rethink (MPGN, C3G, lupus)

**Classification update**: the old MPGN type I/II/III scheme is replaced by IF-based classification — immune-complex MPGN vs C3 glomerulopathy; **dense deposit disease is now classed under C3 glomerulopathy**
Lupus nephritis ISN/RPS: I minimal mesangial, II mesangial proliferative, III focal (<50%), IV diffuse (≥50%; commonest & most severe), V membranous, VI advanced sclerosing (≥90%)
Anti-GBM antigen: NC1 domain of the **α3 chain of type IV collagen**; treat plasma exchange + steroids + cyclophosphamide

Amyloidosis: Congo red apple-green birefringence under polarised light; nephrotic, large kidneys

traps.stem: 22-year-old with cola-coloured urine starting the day after a sore throat; C3 and C4 normal.
traps.fix: Synpharyngitic haematuria (within 1–2 days) with normal complement = IgA nephropathy. PSGN has a 1–3 week latent period and low C3.

traps.stem: MPGN pattern on biopsy, very low C3, normal C4, C3-only IF, ribbon-like intramembranous deposits.
traps.fix: Dense deposit disease — now within C3 glomerulopathy: alternative pathway dysregulation (C3 nephritic factor / factor H). Immune-complex MPGN has IgG + C3 and low C4.

traps.stem: What cells form the crescent in RPGN?
traps.fix: Parietal epithelial cells of Bowman's capsule + infiltrating monocytes/macrophages, stimulated by fibrin.

cards.front: Match the EM/silver finding: (1) spike and dome (2) tram-track (3) subepithelial humps (4) intramembranous dense ribbon (5) effacement only with normal LM.
cards.back: (1) Membranous nephropathy (2) Immune-complex MPGN (mesangial interposition) (3) PSGN (4) Dense deposit disease — C3 glomerulopathy (5) Minimal change disease.

cards.front: Which GN have low C3, and how does C4 split them?
cards.back:
Low C3 + low C4 (classical pathway): lupus nephritis III/IV, immune-complex MPGN (HCV/cryoglobulinaemia), endocarditis/shunt nephritis.
Low C3 + normal C4 (alternative pathway): PSGN (transient, normalises in 6–8 wk), C3 glomerulopathy incl. dense deposit disease (persistent, C3 nephritic factor).

cards.text: Tea-coloured urine the day after a sore throat, normal C3/C4 → {{c1::IgA nephropathy}}; biopsy IF shows {{c2::mesangial IgA}}; if haematuria began 2 weeks after pharyngitis with low C3 → {{c3::post-streptococcal GN}}.

cards.front: RPGN classification by immunofluorescence with prototypes.
cards.back:
Type 1 linear IgG: anti-GBM / Goodpasture (α3 chain type IV collagen).
Type 2 granular immune complex: PSGN, lupus, IgA/HSP, MPGN.
Type 3 pauci-immune: ANCA vasculitis — GPA (PR3/c-ANCA), MPA (MPO/p-ANCA), EGPA.

cards.text: Earliest EM change in diabetic nephropathy = {{c1::GBM thickening}}; pathognomonic LM lesion = {{c2::Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules (nodular glomerulosclerosis)}}; arteriolar lesion = {{c3::hyaline arteriolosclerosis of afferent and efferent arterioles}}.
